title: How would you actually stress test an AI-written trading strategy before trusting it?
author: Vegetable-Rub-8241
selftext:
Been reading a bunch of threads here this week (the Robinhood agentic AI one, the backtesting-with-LLMs one) and one thing keeps showing up: people trust a strategy because the backtest looked good, not because anyone checked whether the good numbers would survive data the strategy never saw.

Full disclosure since it is relevant here, I am building a tool around exactly this problem. You describe a trading idea in plain English, it does the quant work and builds a backtested strategy, and then a separate deterministic step, not the AI itself, grades the result on data it never touched during building. The point is to catch curve fitting before real money does.

What I actually want from this post is not signups, it is your process. If you already stress test your own or an AI's strategies before trusting them, how do you do it? Walk forward windows, out of sample splits, live paper trading for X weeks, something else? And what made you trust the first strategy you ever kept, if any?

Blunt answers and "your whole approach is wrong" answers both welcome.

comments.author: do0fusz
comments.body: Good question. What does ai say?

replies.author: Vegetable-Rub-8241
replies.body: fair meta-question. asked one directly just now: it listed walk forward windows, out of sample splits, and paper trading for a few weeks, all correct textbook answers. what it did not do is tell me which one fits my actual data size or say "this strategy specifically looks fragile." it can list the methods, it cannot grade your result with them. that gap is kind of the whole post.

comments.author: fomoz
comments.body: I don't think your product will survive without showing any PnL. Just my $.02, there are dime a zone apps like these since people started using Claude Code.

replies.author: Vegetable-Rub-8241
replies.body: fair, and the flood of Claude Code trading apps this year makes that skepticism earned, most of them are a screenshot of one good week. that's actually why I'm not leading with a PnL number. a single track record is trivial to cherry pick or get lucky with, and I'd rather be honest that a short PnL screenshot proves close to nothing than post one to look legit. the part I think actually differentiates this is the grading step itself, showing you why a strategy's backtest should or shouldn't be trusted before any real money or time is on the line. long run, yes, a live track record has to be the real proof eventually. what would make you trust a PnL number if you did see one, a minimum time window, a minimum number of trades, something else?

comments.author: engineering-AF7
comments.body: Paper trading + patience is the only thing I can recommend

replies.author: Vegetable-Rub-8241
replies.body:
Hard to argue with. Patience is the part everyone skips and it is the part doing the work.



Two things I never know how to set there. How long is long enough to be a real test but short enough that you have not just measured one regime. And paper fills flatter you, so the slippage lesson always arrives late.



How do you call it? Time, trade count, or just when it stops surprising you?

comments.author: tradematesHQ
comments.body:
The approach you're describing—separating the AI strategy generation from a deterministic out-of-sample validation step—is exactly the right way to think about it. Walk-forward windows and out-of-sample splits are the standard quant methods, but the real issue is that most people stop at "the backtest looked good" without ever checking whether the strategy's logic actually held up on data it never saw during construction.



For stock-level analysis, there's a platform called [trademates.co](http://trademates.co) that does something conceptually similar but for individual stock picks rather than full trading strategies. It freezes an immutable snapshot of the score and verdict at the moment you run an analysis, then checks forward performance at 30/90/180/365 days against a benchmark (SPY or URTH). When a call goes wrong, a second AI pass digs into why—earnings surprise, macro shock, missed catalyst—so you get the post-mortem, not just the number. It's not a strategy builder, but the same principle of separating the evaluation from the generation applies.

replies.author: Vegetable-Rub-8241
replies.body:
Snapshot at analysis time is the part of that I actually like. Freezing the verdict before the outcome exists is the only way a track record cannot get quietly rewritten later.



The second AI pass explaining why a call went wrong is where I would push back. An LLM will always produce a plausible reason after the fact and you cannot falsify it. That is narrative, not evaluation. Forward checking at 30 and 90 days is honest but slow, and each call is a sample of one.



Are you using it yourself or involved with it? Either is fine, just changes how I read the recommendation.



Still after the original thing though: what do you do before you trust something?

replies.author: tradematesHQ
replies.body:
You are right to push back on the second AI pass. An LLM will always generate a plausible-sounding reason, and you cannot falsify it—that is narrative, not evaluation. The forward checks at 30/90/180/365 days against a benchmark are the honest part, but as you said, each call is a sample of one and it is slow but after 7 months you have enough data points to actually make really good decisions. Specially because the you have semantic explanations of what went different and not only statistical data.

Before I trust anything, I do three things. First, I run the strategy on completely unseen data—a time period I deliberately held back during development. Second, I paper trade it for at least 50 to 100 signals to see how fills and slippage actually behave, because backtests always flatter you there. Third, I look for a logical reason the strategy should work, not just a statistical one—if I cannot explain why the edge exists in plain market mechanics, I do not trust the backtest numbers.
